column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: How many dots belong in the electron dot diagram for Mg?
column28: Magnesium is in group 2, so it has 2 valence electrons. A dot diagram shows only valence electrons: 2 dots.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: What is the oxidation number of potassium (K)? Include the sign. Oxidation number: ___
column28: Potassium is in group 1. It loses its 1 valence electron, so its oxidation number is +1.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: The bar chart shows each element's valence electrons. Which element will most likely GAIN 1 electron when it bonds?
column28: Fluorine has 7 valence electrons, so it needs just 1 more to reach a full outer level of 8.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: Sodium forms an ion. Which noble gas does that ion end up matching?
column17: none of them — it stays neutral
column28: Sodium has 11 electrons. It loses 1 to form Na⁺, leaving 10 electrons, the same arrangement as neon.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: Where does an element's oxidation number come from?
column14: Its group on the periodic table — how many electrons it gains or loses
column28: The group tells you the valence electrons, and so how many electrons the atom gains or loses to get a full outer level. That number is the oxidation number.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: Look at the Mg row of the table. Two values are missing, but type only ONE answer: the ION CHARGE of Mg, with its sign (+ or −). Do not type the valence electrons. Ion charge: ___
column28: Magnesium is in group 2, so it has 2 valence electrons. It loses both, giving an ion charge of +2. Only the charge goes in the box.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: An atom that GAINS electrons becomes…
column28: Electrons are negative, so gaining them gives the atom a negative charge: an anion. The number of protons does not change, so it is still the same element.

column4: Why atoms bond and electron dot structures
column9: Which element will NOT normally form a compound?
column28: Argon is a noble gas. It already has a full outer level of 8 valence electrons, so it has no reason to gain, lose, or share electrons.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: Name for KBr?
column28: Name the metal first (potassium), then the nonmetal with its ending changed to -ide (bromide).

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: The arrows show electrons moving as an ionic bond forms. Count the arrows. What charge does each oxygen ion end up with? Include the sign (+ or −). Charge: ___
column28: Two arrows mean oxygen gains 2 electrons. Each electron is negative, so the oxygen ion has a charge of −2.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: Which formula stands for the hydroxide ion?
column28: Hydroxide is OH⁻. (CO₃ is carbonate, SO₄ is sulfate, NO₃ is nitrate.)

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: Use the table to find the charge on the metal ion in Fe₂S₃, then name the compound.
column28: Three sulfide ions at −2 each make −6. Two iron ions must add up to +6, so each is +3: iron(III) sulfide.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: Which pair would form an IONIC bond?
column28: Ionic bonds form between a metal (potassium) and a nonmetal (bromine). The other pairs are all nonmetals, which share electrons.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: What is the charge on the phosphate ion? Include the sign. Charge: ___
column28: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, so its charge is −3.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: What charge does the potassium ion carry? Include the sign. Charge: ___
column28: Potassium (group 1) loses its single valence electron, giving it a +1 charge: K⁺.

column4: Ionic bonds and naming ionic compounds
column9: Name for CuF₂?
column28: Each fluoride is −1, so two make −2. The one copper ion must be +2. Copper is a transition metal, so its charge goes in the name: copper(II) fluoride.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: How many atoms does the prefix "octa" stand for?
column28: Octa means 8, like an octagon has 8 sides.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: How many LONE pairs (pairs of dots that are NOT shared) are in this electron dot structure of F₂?
column28: Each fluorine has 3 pairs of dots that are not in the bond: 3 + 3 = 6 lone pairs. The line between the atoms is the one shared pair.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: Write the formula for phosphorus pentachloride.
column28: Phosphorus has no prefix, so 1 P. Penta means 5, so 5 Cl: PCl₅.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: As bonds go single → double → triple, the bond gets…
column28: More shared pairs pull the two atoms together more tightly, so the bond is stronger and shorter.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: Name CO.
column28: 1 carbon (no mono on the first element) and 1 oxygen = monoxide. Carbon monoxide.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: A double bond means the two atoms share…
column28: Double means 2 shared pairs. Each pair is 2 electrons, so 4 electrons in all.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: What kind of bond does the picture show forming?
column14: No bond — the atoms stay apart
column15: Metallic — electrons drift among many metal atoms
column28: The arrows show each sodium atom giving its electron to sulfur. Electrons moving from a metal to a nonmetal is an ionic bond.

column4: Covalent bonds and naming covalent compounds
column9: Name N₂O. (Both elements need a prefix here.)
column28: 2 nitrogen = dinitrogen; 1 oxygen = monoxide. Dinitrogen monoxide.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: A white solid melts at 850 °C and conducts electricity in water. It is most likely…
column28: A high melting point and a solution that conducts electricity are both signs of an ionic compound.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: The subscript 2 in H₂O tells you…
column15: There are two hydrogen atoms in the molecule
column28: A subscript counts the atoms of the element just before it: 2 hydrogen atoms in each water molecule.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: Does a covalent compound dissolved in water usually conduct electricity?
column14: Only if it is a gas
column17: No — there are no free ions
column28: Covalent compounds are made of neutral molecules. With no ions free to move, there is nothing to carry the current.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: Ne is…
column16: A mixture of two different substances
column28: Ne is one symbol with no subscript and nothing bonded to it: a single neon atom. Neon is a noble gas, so it does not bond.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: Which compound is made of a metal and a nonmetal?
column28: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so MgO is ionic. The other three are made only of nonmetals.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: Which kind of compound does this describe: low melting point?
column28: The forces between separate molecules are weak, so covalent compounds melt at low temperatures. Ionic compounds have high melting points.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: Why can't you have a 'molecule' of NaCl?
column15: NaCl is not a real compound
column17: Ionic compounds form a whole lattice, not separate molecules
column28: In an ionic compound every ion is attracted to all of its neighbors, building one big crystal lattice. NaCl gives the ratio of ions, not a separate molecule.

column4: Comparing ionic and covalent compounds
column9: A clear liquid boils at 78 °C and does not conduct electricity at all. What is it most likely, and why?
column14: Ionic — low boiling point means weak ionic bonds
column15: An element — compounds cannot be liquids
column17: Covalent — low boiling point and no ions to carry a current
column28: A low boiling point and no conduction both point to a covalent compound: separate molecules and no ions.
